gigs.title: Principal Software Engineer
gigs.shortDesc: Architected and built a 12-repository, multi-service platform in Rust and Python — 406 commits, 135,000+ lines of application code, 37 REST and WebSocket endpoints, and two production-shaped data pipelines including a cited, locally-run large language model (LLM) retrieval-augmented generation system measured against a 130-question held-out evaluation set.
gigs.longDesc: Designed and delivered the Brightwater Analytics, Inc. platform end to end: a shared rules-engine library consumed by five services, a 26-route Actix-web API gateway with WebSocket subscriptions, an RS256 OIDC (OpenID Connect) authentication service backed by PostgreSQL and Redis, a GitOps deployment repository running under Kubernetes and ArgoCD, and two independent ingestion pipelines. Worked from written specifications throughout — 15 design proposals with high-level and low-level detail, a decisions log tracking 19 open questions with options and constraints, and 17 numbered architecture revisions — translating product requirements into technical designs before implementation. Enforced object-oriented and type-driven design patterns across a 3,250-file workspace with compile-time modularity: 17 build features and 17,642 conditional-compilation sites let each service compile only the subsystems it needs, sized against a deliberately constrained reference machine. Practiced disciplined defect triage and root cause analysis on machine-generated data — tracing 22 license misclassifications, a challenge-rating experience-point calculation bug, a cross-edition index leak, and 56 CSV rows damaged by a quoting defect back to their causes and fixing the tooling so each class of failure could not recur. Built the generative AI surface as an engineering system under explicit AI governance: a four-stage Python document pipeline feeding large language models (LLM) retrieval-augmented generation with mandatory citation and provenance, retrieval abstracted behind a single swappable interface with both a lexical (SQLite FTS5/BM25) and an embedding-based lane, prompt engineering via prompt templates read from version control at runtime so documented and executed prompts cannot drift, capped and time-bounded local model inference on CPU-only hardware, a 130-question held-out evaluation set, and a standing architectural rule that no AI-dependent path may block the user or run without a deterministic fallback.

blurbs.Software Engineer: Architected a multi-service platform (microservices) in Rust across 12 repositories and 406 commits, applying object-oriented and type-driven software design patterns, data-structure and algorithm work, and compile-time modularity (17 build features, 17,642 conditional-compilation sites) as part of a disciplined systems design practice. Produced high-level and low-level technical design documentation before implementation — 15 written proposals with open questions resolved in writing, a 19-question decisions log, and 17 numbered architecture revisions — including reversing an edition-split architecture after the evidence showed it cost more than it returned. Held a hard quality baseline: zero-warning linting, enforced formatting, and a five-variant compile matrix required before any commit touching the core system module. Specified the architectural contract for the creature decision library before writing its code: a one-way dependency direction (shared rules library to decision layer to consumers), an explicit non-ownership rule barring it from redefining any type already existing upstream, a governance rule requiring an upstream proposal rather than a fork when a needed type nearly fits, three named consumers, and a twelve-phase plan deliberately deferring implementation to phase nine. Built the measurement apparatus before the problem appeared — the multi-user load and benchmark harness for the vertical slice landed the same day as the client itself, ahead of the concurrency failure it would later expose, making the subsequent redesign instrumentation overruling a design rather than a bug fix.
blurbs.Back End: Built five backend services in Rust on Actix-web, exposing a REST API and WebSocket surface: a 26-route API gateway with WebSocket subscriptions, room and invitation lifecycle, message and notes APIs with per-role authorization filtering, and player heartbeats; an authentication service issuing RS256 JSON Web Tokens (JWT) as an OIDC provider with Argon2 password hashing, PostgreSQL persistence via SQL, and Redis caching; plus static-content and server-rendered web services, and a WebAssembly (WASM)-compiled Leptos client consuming the gateway directly from the browser. Designed the canonical shared library every microservice consumes and none reimplements. Engineered the AI surface as a backend concern — retrieval behind one swappable interface, model calls capped and time-bounded, prompts loaded from version-controlled files at runtime, and a deterministic fallback required on every AI-dependent path. Load-tested the gateway on constrained reference hardware, found the per-user connection pool failed near six concurrent users, and replaced it with a stateless per-request design — the fix removed 673 lines and added 256. Split third-party book data across two repositories so a licensing constraint was enforced by construction rather than by discipline: one repository carries the type shapes, per-book build features and empty tables — versioned, reviewed and shareable — while the licensed content those shapes describe is mechanically barred from entering version control by a pre-commit hook and gitignore, and is populated only at run time on a machine holding the source material.
blurbs.Data: Built and operated two ETL (extract/transform/load) pipelines over licensed third-party content, 20 Python modules and 4,932 lines across the ingestion toolchain, with data modeling for a 20+ entity-type relational schema. The first generates typed, license-classified code from three upstream datasets, with per-row classification against two specification versions, a 164-entry alias layer resolving cross-source naming conflicts, and proven idempotency against a merged baseline. The second is a four-stage document pipeline — extraction with 14 per-publisher layout strategies, rules-first shape classification, indexing, and evaluation — converting publisher PDFs into provenance-tagged chunks across 19 books and 2,950 chunks, serving citation-bearing answers from a locally-run model. Designed retrieval as a swappable backend rather than a committed dependency: one entry point, a SQLite FTS5/BM25 full-text search lexical lane as the default and an implemented vector search embedding lane (nomic-embed-text, 768-dimension vectors, brute-force cosine), with the choice to defer sqlite-vec documented against its real cost — regenerating a hash-locked lockfile and moving a supply-chain security `exclude-newer` cutoff. Ran model evaluation rather than asserting quality with a 130-question held-out evaluation set across 13 books, reproducible runs, and stage-to-stage count-agreement assertions that fail loudly on silent data loss. Root-caused and fixed 22 license misclassifications, a calculation bug, a cross-edition index leak, and 56 quote-damaged rows, hardening the tooling against each.
blurbs.Administrator: Maintained a 3,250-file, 12-repository workspace as one coherent system: zero-tolerance lint and format gates, a five-variant per-edition compile matrix before every core-module commit, warning count driven from 2,518 to 2,032, and 437 files brought into format compliance in a single pass. Ran the tracking substrate that made a 1,592-item campaign finishable — a 2,901-row object inventory, status accounting, and ingest logs, with unresolved items error-logged rather than dropped. Managed submodule pointer hygiene across seven submodules, dependency-path migrations, and filename-convention migrations across hundreds of files without data loss. Applied supply-chain controls as policy: hash-pinned dependencies with a time-based cutoff, authenticated dependency clones in continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD), Docker-containerized services deployed via Kubernetes and ArgoCD (GitOps), and pre-commit controls preventing licensed content from entering version control. Ran a cross-machine configuration substrate as version-controlled infrastructure: global directives and per-project memory synchronized automatically between workstations, with a machine roster and working conventions maintained as committed rules rather than local settings.
blurbs.Consulting: Ran the engagement so that nothing significant was decided in passing: a decisions log carrying 19 numbered open questions with context, options, constraints, and a locked / open / parked status — including items deliberately parked rather than resolved prematurely. Established a proposal → review → decision → bake-in workflow, with applied proposals removed so the staging area never misrepresented what was live. Produced stakeholder-actionable artifacts: a phased roadmap, competitive positioning, a business model with licensing posture, and storage-tier tradeoffs marked locked or provisional. Evaluated emerging technology against measured cost rather than reputation — deferring a vector-database dependency after pricing it against a millisecond-scale brute-force scan and a supply-chain cutoff it would have forced. Flagged discovered inconsistencies with evidence for triage instead of fixing them unilaterally. Drew the boundary between deterministic logic and the language model explicitly and in writing before either was built: the creature decision layer is specified as the non-LLM layer, where a deterministic library returns what a creature does given its circumstances and the model is confined to narrating that result — scoping the model out of the decision path rather than reaching for it because it was available. Treated a legal constraint as a first-class design requirement, turning “this material may not be redistributed” from an operating caution into an architectural property of the system.
blurbs.Team Lead: Built the onboarding surface a second engineer would need before there was one: 118 documents totaling 54,930 lines — contributor guides, per-service tactical guides layered under a strategic source of truth, implementer playbooks written for someone absent from the design conversation, runbooks, and procedures. Defined standards and enforced them mechanically rather than socially. Ran multi-agent AI orchestration with written agent specifications, pass tracking, and status accounting to drive batch work across thousands of generated files, with automated formatting and zero-warning linting as the gate every batch had to clear. Built and maintained the operating system for the engineering practice itself, across machines and over five months: a dedicated configuration repository carrying global working directives, per-project memory, a task-tracking system with index/rules/template structure, six LLM-integration planning documents, a machine roster, session-summary conventions, and a source-of-truth convention separating strategy from per-repository tactics — governance written as enforceable rules and synchronized automatically between workstations.

blurbs.Software Engineer: Sole developer of a Zend Framework 2 application whose data layer was Jira rather than a database. Designed a query builder and repository abstraction over JQL so the rest of the system, and everyone who later maintained it, worked against ordinary domain objects instead of Jira queries. Delivered roughly 80 percent of a written specification in four and a half months and documented structures and conventions in code as the work progressed, which is why development continued uninterrupted after the contract ended.
blurbs.Back End: Built the PHP and Zend Framework 2 layer that made a brand-new Jira-backed CMS workable for Northfield Retail Corporation. With no relational store of its own, the application communicated entirely with Jira over its REST API, making the backend an integration and domain-modeling problem rather than a persistence one: a query builder translated domain requests into JQL, and a repository layer kept that translation in a single place.
blurbs.Data: Modeled Northfield Retail Corporation content and workflow as Jira issues, retrieved through JQL by a query builder with a repository layer isolating those queries from the rest of the application. The system held no database of its own. Jira was the system of record, and every read and write travelled through its REST API.
blurbs.Front End: Built the browser-facing editing experience in JavaScript and jQuery: form-driven authoring, WYSIWYG editing, and content previews, used daily by the content team and later by several hundred people across multiple Northfield Retail Corporation departments.
blurbs.User Interface: Designed and implemented the interface that made a Jira backend invisible. Content authors worked with forms, a WYSIWYG editor, and previews, never with issue keys or query syntax.
blurbs.User Experience: The governing design goal was that the exotic backend never surface. Content staff had no reason to know their work was stored as Jira issues, and none of them needed to learn Jira Query Language to do their jobs. That abstraction is what allowed the tool to be adopted across multiple departments by people who were not engineers.
blurbs.Team Lead: Trained the incoming contractor across the final month of the engagement; he completed the remaining scope without interruption once the contract closed. Separately taught Northfield Retail Corporation's content team git and the PHP templating system, so non-engineers could write and wire their own partials and components rather than queuing every change behind a developer.
blurbs.Consulting: Engaged as a contractor against a product owner's written specification, working solo inside an existing content team. Transferred knowledge continuously rather than through a formal handoff, and left a documented codebase a successor could pick up. There was no acceptance gate and none proved necessary.
blurbs.Business: Catapult displaced a legacy content management tool that Northfield Retail Corporation estimated had been costing millions of dollars in time and labor. Seven weeks after the contract closed, a Northfield Retail Corporation developer on the project described the tool as incredibly successful and scaling well as the project grew at an enterprise level.
blurbs.DevOps: Helped configure and deploy the shared development server and maintained the codebase in a shared GitHub repository, establishing the working setup that both the content team and the successor contractor developed against.
